channel.title: Ocufuse Blog
channel.description: Practical guides on eye exercises, eye symptoms and preparing for eye appointments.

item.title: Vision changes with age: what's common, what to check
item.description: Reading glasses and slower adjustment to the dark are common with age. Changes eye care bodies describe, and how often to get checked.

item.title: How to put in eye drops: a step-by-step guide
item.description: The eye drop technique the American Academy of Ophthalmology describes, a lying-down method for nervous blinkers, and tips for children.

item.title: Eye safety at home: DIY, cleaning and the garden
item.description: Nearly half of eye injuries happen at home. Everyday jobs that put eyes at risk, simple protective habits, and first steps after an injury.

item.title: Screen time and children's eyes: everyday habits
item.description: What eye care and pediatric bodies say about screens and children's eyes, and practical habits for breaks, distance, light and sleep.

item.title: How to read your glasses prescription
item.description: OD, OS, SPH, CYL, AXIS and ADD explained in plain words with a labelled example, and why a contact lens prescription is different.

item.title: What happens during an eye exam?
item.description: A step-by-step guide to a comprehensive eye exam: each test, what it checks, how long it takes, what dilation is like and how to prepare.

item.title: Why do eyes look red in flash photos?
item.description: The red-eye effect is light reflected from the back of the eye. Why it happens, why some photos show it, and when a reflection needs a check.

item.title: The blind spot in your eye: why everyone has one
item.description: Every eye has a small spot that can't see. Where it is, why you never notice it, a quick way to find yours, and when a gap needs checking.

item.title: What does 20/20 vision mean?
item.description: The two numbers in 20/20 and 20/40 explained, what 6/6 means, and the parts of your vision and eye health a letter chart doesn't measure.

item.title: Wildfire smoke and your eyes: what to do on smoky days
item.description: Smoke can leave eyes stinging, red and watery. What health and eye care bodies say, simple steps for smoky days, and when to get help.

item.title: Dry eyes in the morning: why they happen
item.description: Waking with dry, scratchy or red eyes is common. Why eyes dry out overnight, bedroom changes that may help, and when to get an eye exam.

item.title: Tiny moving dots when you look at the sky: what they are
item.description: The tiny bright dots that dart about against a blue sky are white blood cells. What they are and how they differ from floaters and flashes.

item.title: Puffy eyes in the morning: common reasons
item.description: Swollen eyelids on waking are common. Why fluid gathers around the eyes overnight, habits that may help, and when swelling should be checked.

item.title: What to do on a screen break (that isn't another screen)
item.description: Swapping a laptop for a phone isn't much of a break. Simple things to do in 20 seconds, 5 minutes or 15 minutes away from the screen.

item.title: Gaming and your eyes: comfort habits for long sessions
item.description: Long gaming sessions can leave eyes tired, dry and blurry. What an AOA survey found, and practical habits for distance, light and breaks.

item.title: Is it bad to use your phone in the dark?
item.description: Scrolling in bed with the lights off won't damage your eyes, but it can tire them. What eye doctors say, and habits for screens at night.

item.title: How far should your monitor be from your eyes?
item.description: About an arm's length, with the top of the screen at or just below eye level. The distances and angles OSHA, Mayo Clinic and eye care bodies suggest.

item.title: How to watch a solar eclipse safely
item.description: Looking at the sun, even partly covered, can permanently damage the eyes. How to watch an eclipse with certified viewers or a pinhole.

item.title: How to put in contact lenses: steps for beginners
item.description: The steps for putting in contact lenses, how to tell if a lens is inside out, and the hygiene habits that matter most.

item.title: Eye makeup and eye hygiene: everyday habits
item.description: Habits from the American Academy of Ophthalmology and the FDA for applying, storing and removing eye makeup safely.

item.title: When should a child have their first eye exam?
item.description: When eye care bodies recommend checking children's eyes, how a screening differs from a full exam, and signs that shouldn't wait.

item.title: How to describe vision changes to your doctor
item.description: Blurry can mean a dozen things. Words and details that help an eye care professional understand what you see, and how to note them.

item.title: Optometrist vs ophthalmologist vs optician
item.description: Three similar names, three different jobs. Who does eye exams, who handles eye disease and surgery, who fits glasses, and who to see first.

item.title: Can your eye colour change?
item.description: Babies' eyes often darken, and light can change how eyes look. What sets eye colour, and why a real change in an adult's eye needs a check.

item.title: Why do pupils change size?
item.description: Pupils shrink in bright light and widen in the dark. How the pupil reflex works, other everyday reasons, and when a change needs a doctor.

item.title: Nearsighted vs farsighted: what's the difference?
item.description: Which one blurs distant things and which blurs close ones, why it happens, common signs, and how an eye exam checks and corrects each.

item.title: Swimming and your eyes: chlorine, goggles and contacts
item.description: Red, stinging eyes after the pool are common. What chlorine does to the eye's surface, simple swim habits, and why contacts and water don't mix.

item.title: Dry eyes in winter: heating, wind and cold air
item.description: Cold wind outside and heated air inside can both dry the eyes. Simple changes indoors and out, and when winter dryness needs an eye exam.

item.title: Crusty eyes in the morning: what sleep crust is
item.description: Sleep crust forms because you don't blink while asleep. What it's made of, how to clean it gently, and discharge that means a call to your doctor.

item.title: Blurry vision in the morning: why it happens
item.description: Blur on waking that clears after a few blinks is common. Why the eye's surface can dry overnight, what to note, and when to get an eye exam.

item.title: Eye floaters: what they are and when to get help
item.description: Floaters are specks and threads that drift across your vision. What causes them, and the signs that mean you need an eye check the same day.

item.title: Can eye strain cause headaches?
item.description: Headache is a listed symptom of eye strain, but not every headache comes from the eyes. What to note, and which headaches need urgent help.

item.title: Is sitting close to the TV bad for your eyes?
item.description: Sitting close to the TV doesn't damage the eyes, eye doctors say, but it can strain them. Why kids do it and when it's a sign to book an eye test.

item.title: Is dark mode better for your eyes?
item.description: Neither mode suits everyone. What eye care and workplace bodies say about light and dark screens, and how to choose for the room you're in.

item.title: Night driving and glare: why it gets harder
item.description: Headlight glare and slower adjustment to the dark make night driving harder for many people. Why, simple checks, and when to see a doctor.

item.title: Rubbing your eyes: why eye doctors say go gently
item.description: Rubbing tired or itchy eyes feels good for a moment. Why ophthalmologists advise against it, and gentler things to try instead.

item.title: Signs a child may have trouble seeing
item.description: Children rarely say they can't see well; they adapt. The everyday signs eye care bodies say parents and teachers can notice.

item.title: Your family eye health history: what to ask
item.description: Some eye conditions run in families. Which ones to ask relatives about, how to write it down, and why it can change how often you're checked.

item.title: How long does eye dilation last?
item.description: Dilating drops usually wear off within a few to several hours. What affects how long it lasts, what it feels like, and how to plan your day.

item.title: Eye myths and facts: what eye doctors say
item.description: Carrots, crossed eyes, glasses that weaken your eyes and screens that ruin them. What the American Academy of Ophthalmology says.

item.title: Colour blindness explained: types, causes and testing
item.description: Most people with colour blindness still see colour, just differently. What causes it, why it's more common in men, the types and testing.

item.title: What is astigmatism? A plain-language guide
item.description: Astigmatism is one of the most common reasons for blurry vision. What it is, what it can feel like, and how an eye exam checks for it.

item.title: How the eye works: a simple guide to its parts
item.description: From the cornea at the front to the optic nerve at the back: what each part of the eye does and how light becomes the image you see.

item.title: Dry eyes when flying: comfort tips for the cabin
item.description: Cabin air dries the eyes on long flights. What to pack in your hand luggage, contact lens tips and in-flight habits from eye care bodies.

item.title: Eye allergies in pollen season: everyday habits
item.description: Itchy, watery, red eyes in spring and summer are often linked to pollen. Everyday habits from eye care bodies for high pollen days.

item.title: Feels like something is in your eye? Common reasons
item.description: That gritty feeling isn't always grit. Common causes, first aid if something really is in your eye, and when the feeling needs an eye exam.

item.title: Why are my eyes watering? Common reasons
item.description: Wind, dry eyes, allergies and blocked tear ducts can all make eyes water. Common causes from the NHS and Mayo Clinic, and when to get help.

item.title: How often should you take a break from the computer?
item.description: Short and often beats long and rare. What workplace and eye care guidance says about screen breaks, with an example hour.

item.title: Screen glare and brightness: setting up light at your desk
item.description: Reflections and a screen brighter than the room tire the eyes. Simple layout and brightness changes that workplace and eye care bodies suggest.

item.title: How often do you blink, and why do screens change it?
item.description: Most adults blink about 15 times a minute, far less at a screen. What blinking does, what research found about screens, and simple habits.

item.title: Sunglasses and UV: choosing a pair that protects
item.description: A darker lens doesn't mean more protection, and an expensive pair isn't always better. What to look for in sunglasses, according to eye care and public health bodies.

item.title: Reading glasses after 40: what presbyopia is
item.description: Holding your phone further away to read it is one of the most common changes in midlife. What presbyopia is, why it happens, and the options an eye care professional may discuss.

item.title: Myopia in children: why time outdoors matters
item.description: Short-sightedness is becoming more common in children. What a large school trial found about outdoor time, and simple ways to fit more of it into the week.

item.title: How often should you get your eyes checked?
item.description: Many eye conditions don't cause symptoms early on. What UK and US eye care bodies recommend for routine eye tests, and who may need to go more often.

item.title: Contact lens habits that lower infection risk
item.description: Most contact lens wearers have at least one risky habit. The everyday steps eye care bodies recommend, from sleeping and water to cases and solution.

item.title: Dry eyes at work: small changes to your desk and day
item.description: Air conditioning, screens and long meetings can leave eyes dry and gritty by the afternoon. Practical changes to your workspace and routine, and when dryness needs a professional.

item.title: Do blue light glasses help? What the research says
item.description: Blue light glasses are sold for eye strain, sleep and eye protection. A 2023 Cochrane review looked at the trials. Here is what the evidence does and doesn't show.

item.title: The 20-20-20 rule: what a 2023 study actually found
item.description: The 20-20-20 rule is one of the most repeated pieces of screen advice. A small study tested it with break reminders. Here is what changed, what didn't, and what it means for your day.

item.title: Diabetes and your eyes: why yearly screening matters
item.description: Diabetes can affect the eyes long before you notice any change in your sight. Why regular eye checks are recommended, what screening involves, and how to prepare.

item.title: Sleep, screens and tired eyes
item.description: Late-night scrolling, short sleep and tired eyes often go together. What the evidence says about screens before bed, and simple evening habits to try.

item.title: How to photograph your child's eyes for a doctor
item.description: An eye that sometimes turns in or out often behaves perfectly at the appointment. How to capture useful photos and short videos of a child's eyes at home.

item.title: Red eye: when to watch it and when to see a doctor
item.description: Many red eyes are minor, but some need care the same day. The signs that separate the two, and what to note while you wait for an appointment.

item.title: Screen eye strain: causes, habits and when to get checked
item.description: Tired, dry or blurry eyes after screen time? The habits with the best evidence, what blue light glasses really do, and when to get your eyes checked.

item.title: Double vision that comes and goes: what to note
item.description: If you sometimes see double, a few simple observations make your doctor's job easier. What to check, what to write down, and when double vision is an emergency.

item.title: Drooping eyelid: what to record and when it's urgent
item.description: When one eyelid sits lower than before, consistent photos help your doctor. How to take them, what to note, and the warning signs that cannot wait.

item.title: What to tell your eye doctor: symptoms, history, questions
item.description: Eye appointments are short. What to bring, what to describe and which questions to ask, so the things you meant to mention don't get forgotten.

item.title: Dry eye diary: a simple format your doctor can use
item.description: Dry, gritty or watery eyes often depend on the day. A simple diary format that shows the pattern, plus what to bring to your appointment.

item.title: Eye twitching that won't stop: causes and notes
item.description: A twitching eyelid is common and usually settles on its own. What tends to set it off, what to write down, and when it is worth getting checked.

item.title: Why your eye photos look different day to day
item.description: Two photos of the same eyes can look surprisingly different. The everyday reasons why, from light to camera angle, and what they do and don't tell you.

item.title: Eye symptoms that come and go: preparing for your visit
item.description: Some eye symptoms disappear right before the appointment. How to keep a simple record so your doctor can see what happens on the other days.

item.title: How to take consistent eye photos at home
item.description: Light, distance and angle change how your eyes look in a photo. Six habits that make daily eye photos comparable from one day to the next.
